newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian sugar strike to hit production.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian sugar strike to hit production.

text.p: A 24-hour strike called by sugar industry workers in the main Australian producing state of Queensland would have a "not insignificant" impact on 1996 raw sugar production, Ian Ballantyne, general manager of grower organisation CANEGROWERS, told Reuters.

Workers, mainly members of the Australian Workers Union (AWU), have called the strike for Thursday to protest against changes to workers' compensation legislation by the federal government. The strike would disrupt crushing of a record crop and affect the state's 25 sugar mills as well as bulk sugar terminals and sugar-loading facilities, Ballantyne said.
"If the strike goes ahead as planned it will close down all of the sugar mills for not less than 24 hours and in some cases longer and it will be extremely disruptive," Ballantyne said.
"We've got a significant disruption." Maintenance would stop some mills from re-starting Friday, he said.
It was a disruption caused by a political issue, not an industrial issue between the industry and the unions, Ballantyne said.
"That's what makes us even more angry about the issue," he said. "It's not a matter we can address, our hands are very much tied on the matter."
Ballantyne said he could not put a dollar value on the cost of the strike in production terms. But the sugar content of the crop was at its highest in September, he said.
"Any disruption to this crop has the quite dramatic potential to force an extra day to the season. At the end of the day you don't pick up that lost sugar," Ballantyne said.
"With a bit of luck we'll get this cane harvested anyway. But we are eventually putting an extra day on the end of the season and there are losses involved.
"If I said it was A$2 million or A$20 million, I wouldn't know. But certainly it would not be insiginificant," he said.
In many cases if operations had to be wound down before the strike or the mill brought gradually back to production when work re-started, the effect could be 36 hours, he said.
The industry had had moderately good relations with unions for several years but the present strike had no reference to the industry and was called for political reasons, he said.

Queensland, which produces almost all of Australia's sugar crop, expects a record sugar cane crop of more than 37 million tonnes and record raw sugar production of more than five million tonnes in 1996.
